They don't actually do any polling themselves but merely tabulate existing polls and apply a number of statistical analyst tools on these. For example ranking polls in specific orders, or running various simulations etc. And maintain this in every interview that they do.

Any mathematical model you use is only ever going to be as good as the data that you put into it. If you put garbage data in - possibly due to polls being off due to people voting counter to how they polled - then you're going to get garbage results. Even if it might only be slightly off, which I think a lot of the polls were.

And people also misunderstand the nature of polling. They are predictive devices: That is they're calling the odds. If they say that there is a outsiders chance of candidate winning that doesn't mean that the polls are necessarily wrong just that this candidate beat the odds.

To further illustrate they don't run a seperate ballot - which I think a lot of people believe, even when it makes no sense if you think about it - but poll amoung specific focus groups and then extrapolate this data to how the general population votes. That is if you measure the average of a number of bricks after a while you can get a rough idea of how many bricks you need for a wall of a certain distance after you've measured a certain number. In a very loose summary.
